items.stem: Which clause filters rows AFTER aggregation, so you can keep only groups meeting a condition on an aggregate?

options.rationale: Correct: HAVING filters grouped results using aggregate conditions.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot reference aggregates.
ORDER BY sorts results; it does not filter groups.
LIMIT caps the number of returned rows; it does not filter on aggregates.

items.explanation: Correct: HAVING filters grouped results using aggregate conditions.

items.stem: Which statements about a LEFT OUTER JOIN are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: It returns every row from the left table even when there is no match on the right
options.rationale: Correct: unmatched left rows are kept, with NULLs for the right columns.

options.text: Unmatched right-side columns appear as NULL
options.rationale: Correct: columns from the right table are NULL when no match exists.

options.text: It returns only rows that match in both tables
options.rationale: That describes an INNER JOIN, not a LEFT OUTER JOIN.
A join does not deduplicate; use DISTINCT or grouping for that.

items.explanation: Correct: unmatched left rows are kept, with NULLs for the right columns.

items.stem: You run UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.1; with no WHERE clause. What happens?

options.text: Every row in the table is updated
options.rationale: Correct: with no WHERE clause the UPDATE applies to all rows.

options.text: The statement is rejected because WHERE is required
options.rationale: WHERE is optional; omitting it is legal and affects all rows.

options.text: Only the first row is updated
options.rationale: UPDATE affects all matching rows, which here is every row.

options.text: Nothing changes until an index is added
options.rationale: Indexes do not gate whether an UPDATE runs.

items.explanation: Correct: with no WHERE clause the UPDATE applies to all rows.
